title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier with a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic semantic validator. For each intent we produced one shared_initial candidate and compared two treatments: (a) baseline — accept the single candidate; (b) guarded — run the deterministic validator and allow at most one automated repair. Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged verifier passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under our synthetic suite and repair budget the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We archive the preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts. We interpret these results with respect to estimand conditioning (shared_initial), validator coverage, repair budget, and operational deployment policies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness properties—sequencing constraints, reachability, and policy preservation—are operationally critical and are not captured by superficial syntactic checks alone. A common engineering pattern pairs generative models with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) to reduce operational risk. Whether such guarded pipelines materially increase the probability that a proposed change is semantically acceptable depends on: the generator quality, the validator's expressiveness, the permitted repair budget, and, critically, the estimand used to measure benefit.

We preregistered a paired experiment (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) that isolates the deterministic rescue available when the same single LLM candidate is evaluated under two treatments. For each intent the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate using the declared generator (gpt-5-mini) and compared: (a) baseline — accept the single candidate without repair, and (b) guarded — run a deterministic validator and allow at most one automated repair which itself is re‑validated. The primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair?

Our contribution is an artifact‑archived, preregistered evaluation that (1) defines and isolates the shared_initial estimand appropriate to operational policies that bound model calls, (2) reports confirmatory inferential results computed on N = 300 paired intents, and (3) interprets the empirical outcome with attention to ceiling effects, validator scope, and repair‑budget tradeoffs.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and systems papers document active work applying LLMs to NetOps and intent translation [1,2,3]. Tool‑augmented and planner‑centric frameworks enable LLMs to call external validators or simulators and coordinate multi‑step workflows; these architectures motivate guarded generate→validate→repair designs [2,4]. Empirical system reports show that deterministic checks and generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve surface correctness relative to unconstrained generation, but reported magnitudes vary substantially with task distribution and validator coverage [3,5].

Two methodological themes in the literature motivated our design. First, many prior evaluations conflate verifier benefit with benefits that come from resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration; this makes it hard to quantify bounded deterministic rescue attributable to post‑generation checking alone [5]. Second, several authors call for semantically rich benchmarks and validators that express sequencing, reachability, and policy invariants rather than only syntactic/template correctness [6,7]. Our study addresses both themes by conditioning on a single LLM draw per intent (shared_initial) and by using deterministic semantic validation that enforces sequencing and preservation invariants encoded in the task suite.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the confirmatory design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) computed on N = 300 paired intents after applying predeclared inclusion/exclusion rules. The preregistration fixed the confirmatory analysis executor (paired binary test), failure handling rules, and sensitivity analyses prior to the main run.

Task suite and stratification. Tasks were deterministically generated into a synthetic topology suite stratified by difficulty (low/medium/high) with 100 pairs per stratum. Each task encodes the natural‑language intent, initial and expected final device states, sequencing requirements (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), protected interfaces, and preservation invariants. Difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) determined stratum membership and ensured balanced sampling.

Shared_initial protocol and model configuration. To isolate deterministic repair effects from resampling, we implemented the shared_initial estimand: for each pair the pipeline produced one shared_initial candidate using the declared generation model gpt-5-mini; that identical candidate was evaluated in both baseline and guarded conditions. This design removes variance due to additional independent model draws and measures only bounded, deterministic validation and repair applied to the same output.

Validator and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used a deterministic validator that implements the preregistered full intent‑constraint checks: sequencing invariants, required command counts, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants, and forbidden‑template protections for protected interfaces. Scoring is binary: an unflagged candidate is a pass for the estimand. The guarded pipeline permits at most one automated repair attempt; the repair operator is a constrained edit routine limited to localized sequencing and insertion edits (for example, inserting a missing 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). Repair candidates are deterministically re‑validated; continued flags count as failures for the guarded condition in the primary analysis.

Contamination controls, audits, and stopping rules. The preregistration included deterministic contamination detection, negative controls (one intentionally broken control per stratum), and exclusion rules (pairs excluded only if both runs failed due to provider/infrastructure outage). The stop rule required halting if >20% of attempted pairs were excluded due to dual‑call outages. Execution instrumentation audited model calls and stage counts to assure shared_initial reuse and repair budget enforcement.

Inference plan. The primary confirmatory test is a paired binary analysis (McNemar style) producing contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), the absolute paired difference, an exact two‑sided test, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (bootstrap seed = 1729, B = 10000). Secondary stratum tests and additional diagnostics were predeclared as exploratory with multiplicity control applied where appropriate.
sections.results:
Execution integrity and accounting. The preregistered adapter completed the confirmatory run with 600 total episodes yielding 300 complete paired observations under the shared_initial protocol. The empirical model‑call footprint equaled 301 hosted model calls (300 shared_initial generations and one repair invocation), consistent with the enforced repair budget ≤ 1. No pairs were excluded under the preregistered rules and deterministic reconciliation verified consistent episode accounting.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300, i.e., baseline = 299/300 (0.9966667) and guarded = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The predeclared exact two‑sided McNemar test (on discordant counts n10 and n01) returns p = 1.0. The absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (seed = 1729, B = 10000) is [0.00, 0.01]. Because discordance is minimal (m = n10 + n01 = 1), exact inference has limited sensitivity; the bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point in this experimental context.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair detail. Per stratum the tallies were: low baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. Thus the single discordant case lies in the high‑difficulty stratum. That discordant episode invoked the permitted automated repair; validator traces attribute the initial failure to an omitted sequencing step (missing explicit 'admin down' before VLAN/MTU change). The constrained repair inserted the missing sequencing command and the validator subsequently reported the corrected candidate as valid. The single automated repair therefore produced the only observed deterministic rescue. Across 300 pairs the guarded pipeline required only one additional repair invocation, indicating a very small marginal model‑call cost for deterministic rescue under the chosen edit operator and suite.

Contamination and missingness. Predeclared contamination checks and negative controls did not flag anomalies. The run contained no provider/infrastructure failures, no unscorable episodes, and no excluded pairs under the preregistered rules. These facts support the claim that the observed contingency counts reflect the scripted task distribution and the shared_initial protocol rather than execution artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under the shared_initial estimand. The shared_initial conditioning corresponds to operational policies that limit model calls for latency, cost, or governance reasons. Under this estimand the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validation and bounded repair applied to a single candidate; it does not capture benefits from resampling, verifier‑guided regeneration, or interactive steering. In our synthetic suite and with gpt-5-mini, single‑shot generation was near ceiling (299/300), so the marginal observable benefit of the guarded pipeline was necessarily small.

Ceiling effects and pilot omission. The preregistration planned an optional pilot to estimate discordance and calibrate power; that pilot was not run. The main experiment therefore encountered a near‑ceiling baseline that produced minimal discordance (m = 1) and limited power to detect small absolute improvements. This outcome highlights the practical value of small calibration pilots when generator performance is uncertain relative to task difficulty.

Validator scope and failure‑mode dependence. The solitary failure mode was a sequencing omission; other classes such as reachability or ACL semantics were not prevalent in this synthetic suite. The practical utility of a guarded pipeline depends strongly on (a) the deployment distribution of failure modes and (b) validator expressiveness. Richer validators that capture reachability, routing‑policy, or ACL semantics could increase observed rescue rates; conversely, operator policies that forbid automated edits constrain guarded pipelines to detection and escalation rather than autonomous repair.

Repair budget tradeoffs. We intentionally limited automated repair to a single constrained edit to measure bounded deterministic rescue. Allowing iterative repair, richer edit operators, or verifier‑guided regeneration would change the estimand and likely increase rescue but at the cost of additional model calls and different operational risk tradeoffs. Our execution accounting (one repair invocation across 300 pairs) quantifies the low marginal model‑call expense for bounded deterministic rescue in this run and can inform policy decisions about permissible repair budgets.

Operational implications. Organizations should align evaluation estimands with deployment policies. If model calls are tightly budgeted, the shared_initial estimand provides an operationally meaningful bound on deterministic verifier/repair rescue for a single candidate. If pipelines permit multiple model calls or interactive steering, evaluations should be conducted under estimands that allow resampling and verify the incremental rescue achievable under those policies. Finally, the empirical ceiling observed here cautions against extrapolating guarded pipeline value without assessing generator baseline performance on the target task distribution.
sections.conclusion: We ran a preregistered paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. Baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.01]). Deterministic validator+repair rescued a single sequencing omission under the bounded repair budget. The near‑ceiling baseline limits inferential sensitivity to small absolute improvements under the shared_initial estimand. We release the preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to enable follow‑up studies that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task distribution, or repair budget.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and the declared deterministic validator were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit arising from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
